title: 15% fall in gold prices could trigger panic, warn lenders - The HinduBusinessLine
text:
A sharp correction in gold prices after a prolonged rally has begun to strain borrowers and lenders alike, with industry executives warning that repayment stress in the gold loan segment has risen across the banking system. While lenders expect the pressure to ease over the next two quarters if gold prices remain stable, a deeper correction could significantly worsen the situation.

Banks and non-banking finance companies (NBFCs) nearly doubled their gold loan portfolios in the September 2026 quarter compared with a year earlier, riding on an almost 80 per cent surge in gold prices driven by global geopolitical uncertainties. However, as the rally cooled and prices retreated from their peaks, concerns around loan-to-value (LTV) ratios and borrower repayments have intensified.

“The slowdown in prices may be one of the major reasons why loan-to-value (LTV) ratios are increasing,” said Mayank Sharma, head of gold loans at IIFL Finance.

“In Q1 and Q2, the prices have already fallen down 25 per cent from Jan-Feb high. So customers needs time to repay,” said Sharma, adding that borrowers had become accustomed to appreciating gold prices over the last two years and were not repaying loans regularly.

With the value of pledged gold declining, borrowers are increasingly being asked to provide additional margin to maintain regulatory LTV requirements, further adding to repayment pressure.

The strain is also beginning to show up in credit bureau data. According to the latest CRIF report, gold loan delinquencies in the 31-180-day bucket rose to 1.6 per cent in September from 1.3 per cent in June, while the 31-90-day delinquency ratio increased to 1.3 per cent from 0.9 per cent. The deterioration comes even as gold loans remained the fastest-growing retail credit segment, expanding 60.6 per cent year-on-year.

The increase in overdue accounts underscores the repayment pressure that lenders have been flagging amid the recent correction in gold prices.

The stress has been exacerbated by the Reserve Bank of India’s decision to cap bullet repayment gold loans at 12 months, forcing more borrowers into regular servicing schedules.

“Earlier, 100 per cent were not servicing monthly. Now, maybe 25-30 per cent are not servicing monthly. Even missing one installment will become SMA 1,” said KR Bijimon, chief operating officer at Muthoot Finance. He said the industry is undergoing a transition period as borrowers adjust to the new repayment structure. “This readjustment will take another two-quarters to set right,” he said, echoing Sharma’s assessment.

Despite near-term stress, industry executives remain confident that gold prices are unlikely to witness a steep collapse. Sharma believes a moderate correction would be absorbed without major disruption.

“A fall in prices from the current levels by 5 per cent to 10 per cent would be manageable. But if the decline crosses 15 per cent, then panic may set in,” he said.

Analysts broadly share that view. Gold is currently trading on MCX at around ₹1.28 lakh per 10 grams and could decline to about ₹1.20 lakh over the next six months, according to Anindya Banerjee, commodities analyst at Kotak Neo. That implies a correction of roughly 7 per cent, well within what lenders consider manageable.

“We believe gold may need several months of consolidation to absorb the excesses of its earlier rally and establish a more sustainable base,” Banerjee said.

For lenders, the key comfort is that most market forecasts point to a period of consolidation rather than a sharp plunge in gold prices. However, with gold loan books having expanded rapidly over the past year, any correction beyond 15 per cent could test borrowers’ repayment capacity and turn the current adjustment phase into a broader asset-quality concern.
